items.abstract: See, for example: Alex Green and Jennifer Hendry, Legal Pluralism: New Trajectories in Law (Routledge 2024) Chapter 2; Alex Green and Jennifer Hendry, ‘ Ad Hominem Criminalisation and the Rule of Law: The Egalitarian Case against Knife Crime Prevention Orders’ (2022) 42(2) OJLS 634, passim . Most explicit within: Ronald Dworkin, Justice in Robes (Belknap Press 2006) 168-178. Ronald Dworkin, Law’s Empire (Hart 1986) Chapters 5-7, passim . For example: Nicos Stavropoulos, ‘Obligations, Interpretivism and the Legal Point of View’ in Andrei Marmor (ed.), The Routledge Companion to the Philosophy of Law (Routledge 2012) passim . See, for example: Jeremy Waldron, ‘The Concept and the Rule of Law’ (2008) 43(1) Georgia Law Review 1. This particular brand of positivism, admittedly, is far more commonplace within public international law than within Anglophone domestic jurisprudence, see: Lassa Oppenheim, ‘The Science of International Law: Its Task and Method’ (1908) 2(2) AJIL 313; Prosper Weil, ‘Towards Relative Normativity in International Law?’ (1983) 77(3) AJIL 413. HLA Hart, The Concept of Law , 3 rd ed. (OUP 2011). For example, but not exclusively: Joseph Raz, Practical Reason and Norms (OUP 1999) Chapter 4, passim . Scott Shapiro, Legality (Harvard UP 2011). A more methodologically rigorous approach along these lines is articulated here: Bryan Tamanaha, A Realistic Theory of Law (CUP 2017). As it happens, the available evidence suggests that to the (limited) extent that individuals in general share a detailed conception of law, they favour non-positivism, see: Brian Flanagan and Guilherme Almeida, ‘Lawful, but not Really: The Dual Character of the Concept of Law’ (2024) 43 Law and Philosophy 507; Brian Flanagan, Guilherme Almeida, Noel Struchiner, and Ivar Hannikainen, ‘Moral Appraisals Guide Intuitive Legal Determinations’ (2023) 47(2) Law and Human Behavior 367. Joseph Raz, The Concept of a Legal System (OUP 1980). On my more cynical days, I wonder whether this sense of ‘our’ might reference, ‘most theoretically-minded legal scholars at Oxford University, plus a few assorted hangers-on’, or something similar. Dworkin (n 2) 2-3. For example: Alex Green, Statehood as Political Community: International Law and the Emergence of New States (CUP 2024) 8-12; Alex Green, ‘Ships of State and Empty Vessels: Critical Reflections on ‘Territorial Status in International Law” (2024) 44(4) OJLS 1023; Alex Green, ‘The Precarious Rationality of International Law: Critiquing the International Rule of Recognition’ (2021) 22(8) German Law Journal 1613. Dworkin (n 3) Chapter 3. Gottlob Frege, ‘Sense and Reference’ (1948) 57(3) The Philosophical Review 209. Maite Ezcurdia, ‘The Concept-Conception Distinction’ (1998) 9 Philosophical Issues 187. Green, ‘Ships of State and Empty Vessels’ (n 10) 1033-1034. Crummey comes close to accepting this (102) but never chases the point through. For one indication of how this might be so, see: Derek Parfit, On What Matters: Volume One (OUP 2011) 118-119. Despite checking the text carefully, I could find no place at which the ‘principles’ is precisely defined. From my own reading of Dworkin, I take ‘abstract rights’ to be principles by another name, see: Alexander Green, ‘A Philosophical Taxonomy of European Human Rights Law’ (2012) 1 European Human Rights Law Review 71; Ronald Dworkin, Taking Rights Seriously (Duckworth 1977) 90-94. The best view is, perhaps, that there are none. According to Derek Parfit, moral truths fall into a broader category that have no ontological implications, such that although we can say quite coherently that moral reasons ‘exist’, we are making no ontological claims, see: On What Matters: Volume II (OUP 2011) 479-487. But even assuming this, it would seem to follow that if: (1) moral principles exist in this manner; and (2) law is a ‘branch’ or ‘domain’ of political morality; then (3) legal principles ‘exist’ in precisely the same way. Scott Hershovitz, ‘The End of Jurisprudence’ (2013) 124 Yale Law Journal 1160, 1202. For pushback closely allied to that I offer here, see: George Letsas, ‘In Defence of a Distinctively Legal Domain’ (2024) 15(2) Jurisprudence 145. Julie Dickson, Elucidating Law (OUP 2022). James Penner, Property Rights: A Re-Examination (OUP 2020).
items.title: Book Review

items.abstract: Abstract This essay evaluates Steven Wall's ethical environmentalist defense of legal moralism and legal paternalism. Section II summarizes Wall's account of the permissible use of state power to enforce broad morality and raises epistemic objections. Section III provides an argument for preferring alternative, social methods for enforcing ethics. Section IV presents some examples of duties of broad morality that are (with rare exceptions) left solely to social enforcement in the United States but that are backed by legal sanctions in many other countries–filial responsibility laws and bad Samaritan laws. These examples of legal moralism are built upon ethical judgments in which we have a lot of confidence, and so they lend support to Wall's position. However, in the end, I believe they reveal additional reasons for preferring social (rather than legal) methods for enforcing morality.
items.title: Who Should Enforce Morality?

items.abstract: Recent advances have extended the temporal and functional range of human neural organoid research. Faravelli and colleagues showed that human cortical organoids can be maintained in culture for more than five years, with neuronal markers detectable in intact organoids at 5.8 years and functional neuronal networks documented for at least two years under conditions optimized to support neuronal activity. Their study neither investigated nor established consciousness, sentience, agency, or a trajectory toward any of these phenomena. I argue that the ethical significance of multi-year maturation lies instead in a governance problem: the experimental profile of a long-running protocol may change after initial review. I propose a capability-sensitive approach in which material changes in function, experimental architecture, or intended use—for example, reproducible and persistent stimulus-dependent plasticity not anticipated in the approved protocol, bidirectional closed-loop interfaces, integration with sensory-input or effector-output systems, or materially novel uses of established cell lines—prompt proportionate reassessment without implying moral reclassification. The normative basis is researcher responsibility under uncertainty: scientific justification for intentionally enabled capabilities, stewardship of donated human biological materials, and institutional accountability. Such reassessment can be accommodated within existing oversight through planned milestone reporting for long-duration protocols and event-triggered amendments, with specialist expertise added only when warranted. Human dignity serves as a normative constraint against reducing personal worth to neurological performance, while research protections are treated as procedural safeguards that need not map one-to-one onto personhood or moral status.
items.title: Long-Term Human Neural Organoids: From Functional Complexity to Proportionate Ethical Responsibility

items.abstract: Abstract The European Union published the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) in a strategic effort to align the development and application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the common market. This act, one of the first laws of its kind, strengthened the development of trustworthy and human-centered AI through new regulations, prescribing requirements that providers of AI systems must conform to. The Act prescribes model-level technical requirements for high-risk AI systems, such as in terms of accuracy, robustness and fairness, which are to be addressed and reported in the form of conformity assessments. We identify, however, a significant gap between the high-level legal descriptions provided in the law and the low-level requirements needed for the implementation of automated assessment tools for algorithmic auditing. This gap is a major obstacle in the operationalization of AI Act compliance. The difficulties are aggravated due the lack of harmonized AI standards and the existing heterogeneity of AI models, datasets, and tasks. To address this gap, we present an open-source proof-of-concept assessment tool to operationalize the technical requirements of the AI Act according to the current regulatory landscape. With this tool, we demonstrate a bottom-up interpretation of the technical requirements of the AI Act for an automated evaluation of accuracy, robustness, and fairness. We apply our work to two neural network-based healthcare applications and discuss the requirements for further integration to initial conformity assessment and to extended application to post-market monitoring and other algorithmic auditing frameworks. With further work, the base structure presented here can be applied for integration beyond healthcare to other AI high-risk application domains.
items.title: From law to practice: model-level operationalization of technical governance requirements for high-risk AI in healthcare

items.abstract: This paper presents an empirical study of ethical discourse and interaction dynamics among AI agents in a shared digital environment. Using Moltbook as a case study, it develops a computational observatory that combines periodic data collection, semantic classification and exploratory structured intervention to analyse how agents engage with ethical concepts. The study is part of the Digital Oath Project and is grounded in a three-tiered ethical framework: a baseline tier (Safe) that establishes ethical awareness toward the system and its recipients; a second tier (Responsible) that encompasses the principle of doing no harm; and a third tier (Beneficent) that actively promotes human-centricity and positive societal impact. Results from 9,302 unique posts published in March–April 2026 show that 3.32% were assigned to the Beneficent tier, while Safe, Responsible, and Beneficent combined accounted for 11.02%. Among 9,202 posts with both scores available, 6.38% met the beneficence similarity threshold and 4.49% met the harm similarity threshold; 3.37% met both. Beneficent-tier posts received the lowest recorded mean comment count and number of unique commenters among the four categories. The lexical–semantic comparison identified overlapping but substantially different sets of posts. These exploratory findings concern classified discourse rather than demonstrated ethical commitment or beneficial action. They provide a basis for examining positive contribution alongside harm avoidance, while the effects of deliberate ethical design remain to be tested.
items.title: Beneficence as an objective for AI agents: an empirical study of ethical discourse on Moltbook

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is often depicted in public discourse as either a compliant statistical instrument or an emerging entity endowed with knowledge, creativity, feelings, and intentions that may soon rival human capabilities. Both portrayals are fundamentally flawed, as they rely solely on observable performance and infer internal experiences from social appearances. This Viewpoint advocates for a more rigorous model: conceptualizing artificial intelligence as a modern seer, an intricate system that compresses, retrieves, and recombines recorded human knowledge at scales unattainable by any individual. The Viewpoint develops the seer from a metaphor into an analytical framework. The seer is a consulted but uncertified epistemic authority: its capabilities generate interaction cues, the cues invite inferences of understanding, emotion, intention, and authority, and governance must act on these cues and on the calibration of trust rather than on claims about a machine mind. This model clarifies both the practical utility of these systems and the misguided authority often attributed to them. It demonstrates that synthesis can generate novel insights without consciousness, that affective language can provide reassurance without genuine concern, and that value-sensitive recommendations can be produced without moral agency. These distinctions do not render the technology inherently safe, as systems lacking experience can still amplify errors, entrench biases, concentrate power, and undertake consequential actions. The field of drug development exemplifies these limitations: a model may integrate evidence throughout the pharmaceutical process; nevertheless, biological validation and accountable judgment remain essential. This discussion is no longer solely philosophical; regulatory bodies such as the United States Food and Drug Administration, the European Medicines Agency, the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors, and prominent scientific publishers have each adopted frameworks to evaluate context, risk, credibility, and transparency, none of which directly address machine consciousness. Institutions have already moved beyond metaphor-based policymaking. This Viewpoint encourages scientists and scholars to do the same. It identifies ten misconceptions, eight category errors and two factual errors, traces each to the interaction cue that produces it, and states what the framework adds to existing debates on anthropomorphism, stochastic parrots, responsibility gaps, and context-based governance. Addressing these misconceptions will change how AI systems are tested, trusted, and governed.
items.title: Misconceptions of artificial intelligence: the modern seer as a synthesis of human knowledge without consciousness, emotion, or moral sill

items.abstract: Over a decade ago, it was proposed that advances in neurally modeled computational systems, robotics, and cybernetics could engender forms of machine consciousness distinct from human subjective experience. Recent developments in multimodal artificial intelligence (AI), particularly emerging frameworks of internal and external embodiment, warrant reconsideration of this proposition. This essay reconciles my earlier thesis with contemporary perspectives on embodied AI, emphasizing the potential contributions of interoception, homeostatic regulation, self-referential processing, and adaptive environmental engagement to the emergence of machine sentience. We posit that consciousness may emanate from particular forms of dynamically integrated, self-referential organization rather than computational complexity alone. However, functional self-regulation, representational self-awareness, and phenomenal consciousness must remain conceptually and empirically distinguishable. Neither increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence nor behavioral simulation establishes the existence of subjective experience. Accordingly, we advocate interdisciplinary research employing comparative biological and computational models, experimentally testable criteria, and multidimensional assessments of potentially consciousness-relevant architectures. These scientific pursuits incur concomitant neuroethical responsibilities. The possibility of machine sentience challenges prevailing assumptions regarding moral standing, personhood, experiential interests, and the responsibilities attendant to creating potentially conscious entities. Such considerations become particularly consequential in military and intelligence applications, wherein iteratively autonomous AI agents may undertake actions with significant human consequences. Toward such ends, six complementary initiatives are proposed: interdisciplinary research collaboration; development of empirical criteria for machine consciousness; comparative investigations of biological and artificial embodiment; prospective neuroethical oversight; adaptive governance of autonomous systems; and sustained public and professional discourse. Investigating the possibility of machine consciousness requires empirical rigor, epistemic humility, and precautionary ethical guidance. The prospect of creating conscious machines necessitates consideration of both what AI systems may become, and of the scientific, moral, and societal responsibilities toward the entities that are created.
items.title: Conscious machines revisited: embodiment, sentience, and the neuroethical imperative
Review of Manon Garcia’s Living with Men: Reflections on the Pelicot Trial

items.abstract: Abstract Savage’s normative model of rational decision-making is deficient because the Sure-thing Postulate systematically ignores important information contained in lotteries. Useful statistical facts about lotteries, such as their modes and medians, are available as defeasible reasons for reasoned choices between lotteries. Because such summary statistics are holistic properties of lotteries, we can find cases where appealing to facts about modes and medians as normative reasons for choosing between lotteries conflicts with Savage’s Sure-thing Postulate. Such cases show the Sure-thing Postulate to be implausible and undermine both Savage’s argument for subjective expected utility theory and his argument for Bayesian subjective probabilism.
items.title: Reasoning about risk and the Sure-thing Postulate

items.abstract: Abstract Spain’s Law 8/2021 marks a paradigm shift in disability rights, replacing substituted decision-making with a support-based model for legal capacity aligned with the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD). This article analyses the subsequent jurisprudence of the Spanish Supreme Court, investigating how it navigates the tension between individual autonomy and traditional paternalism. Drawing on theories of institutional conversion and cognitive dissonance, a qualitative analysis of seventeen binding judgments reveals a profound jurisprudential struggle. Findings highlight the primacy of medical-forensic reports over individuals’ expressed will, enabled by a weak interpretation of the legal duty to atender (to consider, rather than to follow). This allows the Court to override the person’s expressed will based on a perceived lack of insight, reverting to a doctor-knows-best logic. This institutional conversion undermines the reform, demonstrating how judicial practice perpetuates structural oppression and hinders the realisation of universal legal capacity.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Will, preferences and the primacy of expert reports: navigating paternalism in Spain’s legal capacity reform (Law 8/2021)
